hyps.why: Raising a very small learning rate fixes undertraining, whereas raising an already large one overshoots and destabilizes training.
Learning rates near 0.3-1 make Adam diverge, so going further up hurts more than it does elsewhere.
Stepping down from an excessive learning rate restores stable training.
With a tiny learning rate, a larger batch means fewer updates in 243 epochs, so the model is even more undertrained.
Larger batches reduce gradient noise and offset the instability of a high learning rate.
Smaller batches give more update steps, which helps when the learning rate is too small to converge.
Deeper ReLU nets are more fragile at high learning rates, so extra layers add instability.
Widening a narrow network adds needed capacity, with diminishing returns once the network is already wide.
Strong L2 near alpha=1 over-regularizes and underfits, whereas increases in the low range are essentially neutral.
Tiny batches already produce noisy gradients and many steps, so a larger learning rate compounds the noise and destabilizes training.
